husn-dhann.title: “Beware of suspicion”: when doubt is the most false of speech
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
husn-dhann.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ warned his Companions against indulging in bad suspicion of others without evidence, saying: “Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech.” He followed it with a set of related warnings — spying, prying, envying, hating and turning one's back on each other — and commanded them to be brothers.
husn-dhann.historicalContext: One of the concise comprehensive sayings regulating social relationships and preventing hearts from being poisoned by doubts not based on evidence.
husn-dhann.problemType: Falling into bad suspicion of someone close without clear evidence, threatening the relationship
husn-dhann.responseType: A direct warning against believing suspicion, linked to a chain of behaviours that destroy relationships
emotionsAddressed: Doubting the intentions of someone close
Anxiety from interpreting others' actions negatively
principles: Suspicion without evidence can be more false than an outright lie, because behaviour is built on it without verification
Bad suspicion is often the start of a chain leading to spying, envy and estrangement
The default in dealing with others is brotherhood, not distrust
modernApplications: Before building a position on a suspicion or guess, ask yourself: do I have real evidence, or just a feeling?
If you find yourself reading a message or action in the worst possible light, try asking the person directly instead of assuming
Beware of doubt turning into spying or searching for evidence to confirm your bad suspicion
notToApplyTo: This does not mean ignoring real, clear warning signs; the hadith is about suspicion without evidence, not caution based on actual indications
behaviorObservations: He described suspicion without evidence as “the most false of speech”
He linked suspicion to a chain of other behaviours to show it is the beginning of a road, not its end
He ended the guidance with a positive call to brotherhood rather than prohibition alone
whatToAvoid: Confusing thinking well of others with ignoring clear, real signs of an actual problem
husn-dhann.reflection: Much of the pain between people comes not from something that actually happened, but from a suspicion that was never verified.
keywords: i suspect my husband without evidence
i don't trust my reading of other people's actions

quranRefs.context: The Quranic foundation on which the hadith's prohibition of suspicion, spying and backbiting rests
quranRefs.relevance: It describes some suspicion as plain sin, and links it directly to spying and backbiting just as the hadith does

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: This is a general principle he warned against; that is a personal situation he lived himself under the same principle, when false suspicion touched the person dearest to him

thumama.title: Thumamah ibn Uthal: winning hearts through patience, not revenge
participants: Thumamah ibn Uthal (a captive from Banu Hanifah)
thumama.eventDescription: The Muslims captured Thumamah ibn Uthal, a chief of Banu Hanifah who was hostile to the message, and tied him to a pillar of the Prophet's Mosque. Every day the Prophet ﷺ came to him and calmly asked: “What do you have to say, Thumamah?” Thumamah answered with some defiance, and the Prophet ﷺ left him without coercion or haste, until on the third day he ordered him released without ransom. Thumamah went, washed, and returned announcing his Islam of his own free will, saying that there had been no face he hated more than the Prophet's ﷺ, and now it had become the most beloved face to him, after the kindness he had received.
thumama.historicalContext: This happened around the sixth year after the migration, and it is one of the most notable stories of winning hearts through kindness rather than coercion in the Prophet's biography.
thumama.problemType: Dealing with a hostile person or outright opponent in a situation where you hold complete power over them
thumama.responseType: Repeated patience, a calm renewed question, and kindness not conditional on the other side changing straight away
emotionsAddressed: The urge to break or take revenge on a hostile person immediately
Despairing of a stubborn person ever changing
principles: Winning hostile hearts takes time and repeated patience, not one moment
Unconditional kindness has a stronger effect than coercion in changing inner positions
Giving the other side space and respect, even when they are weak, opens a door to change
modernApplications: With a hostile or stubborn person over whom you have the upper hand, try patience and calm repeated questions instead of pressure or coercion
Do not expect someone to change after your first act of kindness; repetition is part of the method
Preserve the other person's dignity even at a moment of weakness before you; this is more likely to win their heart
notToApplyTo: This does not apply to situations of direct danger that require immediate firmness to protect yourself or others
behaviorObservations: He did not hurry Thumamah's change of heart, but left him three days, asking him calmly each time
He released him without ransom or any prior condition of embracing Islam
He did not later remind him of his former hostility
whatToAvoid: Expecting an immediate result from every act of kindness towards a hostile person
thumama.reflection: Sometimes the strongest weapon against hostility is tireless, repeated patience in doing good.
keywords: how to deal with someone hostile to me
a stubborn opponent who won't change
how to win the heart of someone who hates me

quranRefs.context: A general Quranic principle of repelling evil with what is better
quranRefs.relevance: It describes exactly what happened with Thumamah: an enemy who became a “devoted friend” through kindness, not coercion

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: Repeated patience with an enemy until his heart truly changed, versus firm refusal to presume bad intent in another enemy who declared Islam — the difference is in verification, not in the basis of mercy

hunayn-ansar.title: The spoils of Hunayn: when true fairness is misunderstood
hunayn-ansar.eventDescription: After the Battle of Hunayn, the Prophet ﷺ gave from the spoils to some new Muslims to win their hearts, and gave nothing to the Ansar because their faith was firm and needed no winning. Some young men of the Ansar felt hurt at not receiving what others received. The Prophet ﷺ gathered them and addressed them, explaining the wisdom, and said: “Are you not pleased that people go away with sheep and camels, while you go back to your homes with the Messenger of Allah?” They wept until their beards were wet and said: We are pleased with Allah as our Lord and with the Messenger of Allah as our share.
hunayn-ansar.historicalContext: This happened after the Battle of Hunayn in the eighth year after the migration.
hunayn-ansar.problemType: A team or group feeling apparently short-changed, even though the decision is fair in principle
hunayn-ansar.responseType: Addressing the feeling directly through dialogue and explanation instead of ignoring it or relying on the decision being right in principle
emotionsAddressed: Feeling short-changed although there is no actual injustice
Feeling that intangible appreciation is worth less than material reward
principles: A team's feeling of being short-changed deserves to be addressed directly, even if the decision is fair in principle
A wise leader explains the wisdom behind a decision instead of merely imposing it
Symbolic appreciation and deep trust may be more precious than visible material giving
modernApplications: If your team feels short-changed by a distribution decision, do not ignore the feeling even if the decision is fair at heart
Explain the wisdom behind decisions that may look unfair on the surface
Remind the team closest to you of their special place instead of assuming they know it implicitly
behaviorObservations: He did not ignore the Ansar's feelings but gathered and addressed them directly
He reminded them of their long history with him before explaining the current decision
He used a moving phrase comparing symbolic value with material value
whatToAvoid: Assuming a team's feeling of being short-changed will fade by itself without direct dialogue
hunayn-ansar.reflection: Sometimes people do not need the decision changed; they need to feel that someone saw their effort and sincerely valued it.
keywords: my team feels short-changed by the distribution
employees feel it's unfair even though the decision is fair
how to explain a decision that looks unfair to my team

khutbat-wadaa.title: The Farewell Sermon: no one is better than another except by piety
participants: Tens of thousands of Muslims at the Farewell Pilgrimage
khutbat-wadaa.eventDescription: In his last sermon before the largest gathering of his Companions, the Prophet ﷺ established a principle radical for its time, abolishing the usual tribal and ethnic standards of superiority. He said: “O people, your Lord is one and your father is one. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a red-skinned over a black, nor a black over a red-skinned, except by piety.”
khutbat-wadaa.historicalContext: This sermon was delivered during the Farewell Pilgrimage in the tenth year after the migration, a few months before the Prophet's ﷺ death.
khutbat-wadaa.problemType: Discrimination between people on the basis of race, colour or origin
khutbat-wadaa.responseType: A clear and decisive declaration of human equality, naming the only valid criterion of distinction
emotionsAddressed: Feeling discriminated against because of origin, colour or nationality
Feeling superior on an ethnic or tribal basis
principles: Origin, colour or nationality have no bearing on a person's human or religious worth
The only valid criterion of distinction between people is piety and good deeds, an inner matter, not an outward one
Declaring major principles clearly and publicly prevents them from being reinterpreted or evaded later
modernApplications: Review your implicit judgements: do you sometimes assess people based on their origin or nationality without meaning to?
If you face discrimination because of your origin or colour, remember this principle is clear and explicit and leaves no room for reinterpretation
In any position of responsibility, apply the criterion of competence and character, not ethnic or social belonging
behaviorObservations: He chose the largest possible gathering to announce this principle so it would reach the most people
He phrased it decisively, allowing no exception
He tied the criterion to something inner (piety), not to any outward trait beyond a person's choice
whatToAvoid: Using this principle to deny the existence of social or historical inequalities that need separate, practical treatment
khutbat-wadaa.reflection: When people are measured by an inner standard like piety rather than by things beyond their choice, equality becomes a foundation, not a slogan.
keywords: i faced discrimination because of my origin
someone looks down on me because of my nationality or colour

quranRefs.context: Ibn Kathir mentioned in his commentary that this verse is the basis the Prophet ﷺ relied on in his sermon abolishing the pre-Islamic pride in lineage
quranRefs.relevance: It is the direct Quranic foundation for the Prophet's ﷺ words in the Farewell Sermon itself, setting the only criterion of distinction: piety

hadithRefs.narrator: Narrated by many Companions from the Prophet ﷺ in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon

numan-bashir.title: “I will not witness injustice”: fairness between children
participants: al-Nu‘man ibn Bashir (may Allah be pleased with him)
numan-bashir.eventDescription: Bashir ibn Sa‘d wanted to give his son al-Nu‘man a special gift (a servant boy). His wife asked him not to unless he made the Prophet ﷺ a witness to the gift. Bashir took his son to the Prophet ﷺ asking him to witness it. The Prophet ﷺ asked: “Do you have other sons?” He said: Yes. He asked: “Did you give each of them the same?” He said: No. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Then do not make me a witness, for I do not witness injustice.” In another narration: “Be fair between your children.”
numan-bashir.historicalContext: One of the foundational hadith in family law, agreed to be authentic, and a key reference on equality between children in gifts.
numan-bashir.problemType: Favouring one child over another in gifts or attention, unintentionally or with an apparent justification
numan-bashir.responseType: Refusing to take part in any unfair act, even between a father and his children, and clearly directing towards equality
emotionsAddressed: Being unsure whether treating children differently is acceptable for a certain reason
principles: Fairness between children is a foundation of upbringing not to be taken lightly, even if the matter seems small
The Prophet ﷺ refused even to “witness” a favouring act, not just to do it
Favouring one child, even with a small gift, can plant a deep sense of injustice that lasts a long time
modernApplications: Watch yourself when giving gifts, privileges or even emotional attention among your children
If you have a valid reason for different treatment (such as a special health need), explain it to the other children instead of leaving it unclear
Remember that a child's sense of unfairness stays with them for many years, even if the parent forgets it
notToApplyTo: This does not prevent special treatment based on real need (illness, disability) as long as the reason is explained and no favouritism is intended
behaviorObservations: He asked about the other children before agreeing to anything
He refused even to “witness” an unfair act
He asked the father to take back the gift or treat all equally
whatToAvoid: Believing that favouritism is acceptable as long as it is small or not announced
numan-bashir.reflection: When the leader refuses even to be a witness to an unfair act, the seriousness of the matter becomes clearer than any direct warning.
keywords: i favour one of my children over another
my parents favour my brother over me
how to be fair between my children
my brother is my parents' favourite

dog-water.title: Water for a thirsty dog: mercy that includes every living being
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
A man from the Children of Israel
dog-water.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ told his Companions about a man walking along a road who became very thirsty. He found a well, climbed down and drank. When he came out he found a dog panting with thirst, licking the damp earth. The man said: This dog has become as thirsty as I was. He went down the well again, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his mouth as he climbed up, and gave the dog water. Allah thanked him for it and forgave him. The Companions asked: Is there reward for us even with animals? The Prophet ﷺ said: “In every living creature there is reward.”
dog-water.historicalContext: The Prophet ﷺ used this story (an account of an earlier nation he narrated with an authentic chain) as a teaching method to show the vastness of Allah's mercy and that kindness to animals is a cause of forgiveness.
dog-water.problemType: Taking lightly mercy towards animals or weak creatures that cannot claim their rights
dog-water.responseType: Teaching through a story that widens mercy to include every living being, and linking it to forgiveness
emotionsAddressed: Indifference to the suffering of a creature that cannot speak or complain
principles: Mercy in Islam is not limited to humans; it extends to every living creature
Small deeds no one sees may be the cause of great forgiveness
A story is an effective teaching method that stays in the memory more than direct instruction
modernApplications: Widen your circle of mercy to include the weak creatures around you, not only people
Do not belittle a small good deed you do with no reward or witnesses
If you want a moral principle to take root in yourself or others, try telling it as a story rather than a dry instruction
behaviorObservations: He chose a simple, moving story instead of a dry direct instruction
When the Companions asked, he widened the answer to a general principle, not just one incident
whatToAvoid: Interpreting this principle in a way that justifies neglecting human rights in favour of animals
dog-water.reflection: When mercy extends to those with no language to complain in, the picture of true mercy is complete.
keywords: how to deal with a harmful or weak animal
is there reward for kindness to animals

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

hospitality.title: Honouring the guest: a sign of faith
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
hospitality.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ linked the perfection of faith to a set of everyday social manners, saying: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him not harm his neighbour; whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent,” making hospitality, guarding the tongue and not harming the neighbour a practical measure of faith, not just social advice.
hospitality.historicalContext: One of the Prophet's concise sayings that link everyday manners to the reality of faith, not only to social custom.
hospitality.problemType: Neglecting to receive guests well, or seeing hospitality as a burden rather than a virtue
hospitality.responseType: Linking honouring the guest directly to the reality of faith, not to social custom alone
emotionsAddressed: Feeling exhausted or annoyed at hosting others
Falling short in a guest's right without feeling any guilt
principles: Honouring the guest in Islam is a measure of faith, not merely a social habit or courtesy
Simple daily manners (hospitality, guarding the tongue, good neighbourliness) are gathered under one measure: faith
Good hospitality does not require excessive cost, but good treatment and a warm welcome
modernApplications: Review how you receive guests: do you feel annoyed, or honoured, when someone visits you?
Keep hospitality simple and sincere, not so excessive that it strains you financially or emotionally
Link small daily manners (like hospitality) to a deeper meaning than social habit
notToApplyTo: This does not mean straining yourself financially or going beyond reasonable limits in hospitality
behaviorObservations: He combined three social instructions in one connected sentence
He made the standard inner (faith), not outer (custom or courtesy)
whatToAvoid: Seeing good hospitality as a burden instead of a virtue
hospitality.reflection: When the way you receive a guest is measured by your faith, small daily details become part of your relationship with Allah.

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

sila-rahim.title: Keeping ties is not reciprocating: reaching out to those who cut you off
participants: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (may Allah be pleased with them), the narrator
sila-rahim.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ set a precise standard for what truly keeping ties of kinship means. He explained that someone who keeps in touch with a relative because the relative does the same is not keeping ties in the full sense; the one who truly keeps ties is the one who keeps reaching out even to relatives who cut him off. He said: “The one who keeps ties is not the one who reciprocates; rather, the one who keeps ties is the one who, when his ties are cut, restores them.”
sila-rahim.historicalContext: A comprehensive hadith on family relationships, raising the standard of keeping ties from mere exchange to taking the initiative.
sila-rahim.problemType: Estrangement from a relative because they cut you off first, or treating relatives only as they treat you
sila-rahim.responseType: Raising the standard of keeping ties from reciprocation to taking the initiative, even with those who cut you off
emotionsAddressed: Feeling fully justified in cutting off those who cut you off
Tiredness from always taking the initiative with nothing in return
principles: Real ties are tested when the other side cuts you off, not when the exchange is comfortable
Merely returning kindness with the same does not reach the level of “keeping ties” in the Prophetic standard
Taking the initiative despite being cut off is nobler than waiting for the other side
modernApplications: If a relative has cut you off, consider a small step to reach out instead of waiting for them to do so
Do not make “returning favours in kind” the only standard of your relationship with relatives
Remember that reaching out despite estrangement has a completely different value from a balanced exchange
notToApplyTo: This does not mean enduring repeated harm or abuse from a relative; you can keep a minimum of contact while setting boundaries that protect you
behaviorObservations: He clearly distinguished between “reciprocating” and “truly keeping ties”
He made the real test of ties how one acts when cut off, not when connected
whatToAvoid: Confusing keeping ties through initiative with accepting ongoing harm without boundaries
sila-rahim.reflection: The deepest form of connection is not the one returned in kind, but the one given even when the other side does not seem to deserve it.

jewish-boy-sick.title: Visiting the sick Jewish boy: mercy even in calling to faith
subCategories: Dealing with people of other faiths
participants: A Jewish boy who served him
jewish-boy-sick.eventDescription: A young Jewish boy used to serve the Prophet ﷺ. The boy fell seriously ill, and the Prophet ﷺ went to visit him despite the difference in religion. He sat by his head and said to him gently: “Accept Islam.” The boy looked at his father, who was sitting beside him, as if asking permission, and his father said: Obey Abu al-Qasim. The boy accepted Islam before he died. The Prophet ﷺ left saying: “Praise be to Allah who saved him from the Fire.”
jewish-boy-sick.historicalContext: One of the hadith showing the Prophet's ﷺ humane treatment of those who served him regardless of their religion, and his care for their guidance without coercion.
jewish-boy-sick.problemType: Balancing care for someone's guidance or advice with respecting another person's (such as a parent's) right to decide
jewish-boy-sick.responseType: Visiting and personal care, a direct gentle invitation without coercion, while respecting the father's role
emotionsAddressed: Hesitation to visit or care for someone different from you in religion or thought
Over-eagerness that may turn into coercion in giving advice
principles: Human care (such as visiting the sick) does not require agreement in religion or thought
Calling to the truth is done with direct gentleness, not insistence or pressure
Respecting the role of other people involved (like the father here) is part of good manners
modernApplications: Do not hesitate to show human care (visiting, checking on someone) to those who differ from you in religion or thought if you have a relationship
If you want to advise someone close to you, raise the matter gently once and leave them room to decide
Respect the right of others involved in the decision (such as parents) instead of bypassing them
behaviorObservations: He took the initiative to visit despite the different religion, and though the boy was a servant rather than a friend
He made the invitation once, gently, without insistence or pressuring repetition
He respected the father's role and did not bypass him
whatToAvoid: Turning advice into repeated pressure that loses its effect
jewish-boy-sick.reflection: When mercy is wider than the circle of agreement in religion or opinion, it comes closer to the heart of the human message of faith.

a colleague of a different religion is sick
how to advise someone without insisting

zuhd-food.title: Three days in a row: contentment despite the means
participants: ‘A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), the narrator
zuhd-food.eventDescription: ‘A'ishah described the simple living of the Prophet ﷺ at home, although he led a nation growing day by day with wealth and spoils flowing to it. She said: “The family of Muhammad ﷺ never ate their fill of barley bread two days in a row until he passed away.” In another narration: “The family of Muhammad, since coming to Madinah, never ate their fill of wheat bread three nights in a row until he passed away.”
zuhd-food.historicalContext: One of the descriptions conveying the Prophet's ﷺ simple daily lifestyle, despite the expansion of the Muslim state in the last years of his life.
zuhd-food.problemType: Excessive preoccupation with accumulating money, food or luxury even when able to
zuhd-food.responseType: Voluntary contentment with the minimum despite having the means of luxury
emotionsAddressed: Feeling that personal worth is linked to standard of living or consumption
Anxiety about not keeping up with other people's lifestyles
principles: True contentment is tested when you can afford luxury, not when you cannot
Simple living did not stop the Prophet ﷺ from leading a nation and expanding a state
A person's true value is not measured by how much they consume
modernApplications: Review your relationship with consumption: do you buy or eat more than you need just because you can?
Separate real success (impact, achievement) from the luxuries that sometimes come with it
Try practising voluntary contentment in one area of your life even when you could have more
notToApplyTo: This does not mean forbidding good things or requiring poverty; simplicity here was a personal choice, not a general rule imposed on everyone
behaviorObservations: He kept his personal living simple despite the state's expansion and the resources of the spoils
He did not use his position as leader to gain extra personal luxury
whatToAvoid: Thinking that simplicity means rejecting blessings or not being thankful for them; the point is contentment, not deliberate deprivation
zuhd-food.reflection: When contentment is a choice made while able to have more, it becomes a moral value, not an imposed circumstance.
keywords: i feel pressure to keep up with other people's lifestyle
being content with what i have
why do i feel dissatisfied even though i have a lot
